title: A Care-Giver's Trials
author: Special Education Today
summary: This Special Education Today post highlights and excerpts a Washington Post feature by Ariana Eunjung Cha profiling Annie Morgan, a mother whose 13-year-old daughter Ava has Angelman syndrome and requires intensive daily physical support. The excerpted narrative follows a single six-minute struggle to get Ava into the car for school, using granular physical detail (blocking blows, tightening seatbelts, sweat gathering) to convey the constant vigilance and physical toll caregiving imposes on a parent. The Special Education Today author situates Morgan's story within the much larger, often invisible population of family caregivers across the country, from adult children lifting aging parents out of bed to spouses managing medications. The piece closes with an explicit endorsement of the reporting's sensitivity and accuracy, framing the article's value as prompting broader public appreciation for the unseen daily labor of family caregiving. As a Family-bucket entry, the piece centers on the lived reality of parenting and sustaining a household around a child's disability rather than on classroom or school-system concerns.
points: Uses a single six-minute, moment-by-moment account (loading a child into a car) to make the physical and emotional toll of daily caregiving concrete rather than abstract.
Frames one family's Angelman syndrome caregiving story as representative of a much larger, largely invisible population of American family caregivers.
Highlights caregiving's many household forms beyond disability parenting: adult children lifting aging parents, spouses managing medications, and parents dressing adult children.
Endorses the original reporting's sensitivity as a model for how caregiving stories should be told, without sensationalism but with full physical detail.
quotes: Annie Morgan wrapped her arms around her eldest daughter's waist and guided her toward the minivan, the two of them moving in a slow, sideways shuffle.
At 13, Ava was nearly as big as Annie, who stands just five feet flat, 110 pounds.
Then something shifted. As Annie helped Ava into the vehicle, Ava wailed and slammed her body against the seat. The car rocked.
The struggle lasted six minutes: long enough for Annie to tighten one belt, then another. Long enough to block a blow to the head, catch Ava's hands and dodge them when she couldn't.

In one form or another, scenes like this unfold every morning in millions of American homes. Sons and daughters lifting aging parents out of bed. Spouses managing medications. Parents helping adult children get dressed.
Ms. Cha's reporting seems sensitive and accurate to me. I hope that her article prompts people to appreciate the contributions of caregivers to the well-being of our kids.
